newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT-Bob Charles: a New Zealand sporting icon.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT-Bob Charles: a New Zealand sporting icon.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Dec 18 - Bob Charles has been regarded as the best lefthanded golfer in the world for most of the past 40 years, NZPA reports.
Strange then that he has never considered himself lefthanded.
"Goodness no. I'm the most righthanded person you could ever find" he said.
The man who has carried the flag for lefthanded golfers all these years said that actually he is standing "on the right side of the ball" and hitting what would be a backhand to a righthander.
"I am terribly weak on my left side.
"I can't throw and write with my left hand, and I can't kick with my left foot. I'm very lopsided."
He feels that playing lefthanded has not hindered his career.
"There have been problems.
"In the early days especially, there was a shortage of clubs for lefthanders.
"Fortunately for me, both my parents were lefthanders and I inherited their hand-me-downs.
"Coaching manuals were not written for lefthanders and there was no specific coaching for lefthanders.
"So I got the books by Ben Hogan and Sam Snead and while I don't think I ever read a word, I did study the pictures for hours.
"I'd practise into a mirror so I had a mirror image of their swings. That's how I learnt.
"On the other hand, being a lefthander, and especially coming from New Zealand, I was a rarity, so that stood me in good stead.
"I tended to stand out because I was different."

The defining moment of Charles' long career came at Royal Lytham and St Anne's in 1963 when he hammered American Phil Rodgers by eight strokes in the 36-hole playoff to win the British Open, one of the four major tournaments in world golf.
"That victory set me up for my career and is often still referred to, but to tell the truth, I was a little disappointed I never picked up another two or three majors.
"I was second in successive years in the British Open to Gary Player and Tony Jacklin, second in the USPGA to Julius Boros and had several other finishes where I was in contention until near the end.
"Still, a lot of very fine players -- I'm thinking of the likes of Bruce Crampton -- go through their careers without winning a major, so I'm happy with my lot."
Charles burst onto the golf scene by winning the New Zealand Open in 1954 when he was an 18-year-old amateur.
"We drove from the Wairarapa over the Rimutakas to the Heretaunga course each day, and it was a much longer drive in those days.
"I was fairly calm throughout and didn't really feel I'd achieved anything too special, though having an amateur, especially a teenager, win the open, caused some headlines."
Charles remained a leading amateur until 1960. In that time he twice played in the Eisenhower Trophy and showed he was the equal of virtually any amateur in the world.
In 1958 he travelled around the world in the company of former New Zealand cricket captain Ian Cromb, who became something of a mentor for him.
Charles played the US Masters as an amateur and lined up in several big events.
He got a feel for travel and tournament golf and liked the experience.
So two years later he took the plunge and turned professional.
"I had a round-the-world air ticket and about stg 1000 (NZ$2391).
"The idea was that I'd play until I ran out of money and would then return home, my professional career over.
"But I earned some good prizemoney right from the start and comfortably paid my way."
His first big overseas victory was in the 1962 Swiss Open.
The following year he won the Houston Open, a major milestone as it showed he could foot it on the competitive US tour.
Still, to win the British Open was another thing altogether.
"The fields weren't as strong in those days," he recalled.
"I figured all I had to do was beat Palmer, Player, Nicklaus and Peter Thompson and I'd have a good chance."
That assessment is typical of the phlegmatic Charles.
He said that once he'd tied for first with a four-round total of 277, he had no trouble sleeping.
"I've never been a nervy person. I turn up and apply myself. I'm fortunate my concentration is very good when I'm on the course," he said.

Charles won at regular intervals. He claimed several other US tournaments including the Tucson Open (1965), Atlanta Classic (1967) and Greensboro Open (1974), and he was always a threat in Europe where he won the Swiss Open again in 1974, the Scandinavian title in 1973, the Dunlop Masters and John Player Classic in 1972 and the world matchplay title at Wentworth in 1969.
To win the matchplay he not only had to beat Arnold Palmer along the way, but in the final holed putts of 45, 36 and 54 feet on successive greens to beat Gene Littler on the 37th.
Charles won the Canadian Open in 1968, the South African in 1973, four New Zealand Opens and in 1980 the New Zealand PGA title.
In 1990 he became the first golfer to be inducted into the Sports Hall of Fame.
He was a wonderful ambassador for New Zealand golf. Because of him, legends like Palmer and Player ventured to New Zealand for tournaments and exhibitions.
Initially he was famous for his machine-like putting and his precision irons but in more recent years his driving has been the most impressive aspect of his game.
He said he's as New Zealand as ever.
"I'm very proud of being a New Zealander. I have a home in New Zealand, travel on a New Zealand and follow any New Zealand sports results I can find.
"I live in the US for practical reasons, but I have no doubts where my roots are."
Charles continued playing on the regular tours until he turned 50 in 1986.
Then he plunged into the US Seniors tour and began to rewrite the record books.
Encouraged by the success the previous year of Thompson, he set about his new career as an over-50 golfer with gusto, training hard and ensuring he stayed healthy.
He has now won more Seniors tournaments than anyone except Lee Trevino, and has won more prizemoney since turning 50 than he ever did in his years of regular tournament play.
He recently became one of only four golfers to win a seniors tournament at the age of 60.
Through it all, Charles has continued to support New Zealand golf.

He donates a percentage of his tour earnings to the New Zealand Golf Foundation (the total has now topped $100,000), has scholarships set up in his name and is still a major drawcard at the New Zealand Open.
For longevity and qualify of performance, Charles is rightly regarded as a New Zealand sports icon.
